rewrite.question:
What does TypeScript report?

```ts
const f: () => void = () => 5;
```
options: Type error: 5 is not assignable to void
No error; a void return type means callers ignore the result
Type error: an arrow function cannot be assigned to a function type
No error, but calling f() has type number
rewrite.hint: Ask what a () => void type promises to callers, and whether an implementation that hands back extra information breaks that promise.
rewrite.explanation: A function type with a void return is satisfied by any function; the implementation may return 5, and callers typed through f cannot use the result, since f() has type void. This rule is what lets you pass a value-returning arrow, or a method like array.push, to a callback typed () => void. The error appears only when a function declaration is itself annotated : void and contains return 5, because there the annotation applies to the body directly. At runtime f() still yields 5, which is why the types treat the value as ignored rather than absent.

rationale: Key verified and the rule matters for every callback parameter, but the runtime-true distractor makes two answers defensible. Reframing the stem around the checker and replacing that option fixes it.

Nothing is frozen at runtime, so there is no error there either; Object.freeze would be needed for that, and a readonly number[] type removes push at compile time.

rewrite.question:
What does TypeScript report?

```ts
const t: [number, ...string[]] = [1, "a", "b"];
```
options: Type error: a tuple has a fixed length
No error; the rest element allows any number of trailing strings
Type error: "b" has no matching position
No error, but only because t is treated as (string | number)[]
rewrite.hint: Read the tuple type as one fixed first slot plus an open-ended tail. Ask what the tail permits for the second and third values.
rewrite.explanation: [number, ...string[]] means one required number followed by zero or more strings, so [1, "a", "b"] matches, and so would [1]. The rest element keeps the tuple a tuple: t[0] is still number and t is not downgraded to (string | number)[]. A second number, as in [1, 2], is rejected with TS2322. This shape, one fixed element plus a tail, is how a non-empty array type such as [T, ...T[]] is written.

rationale: Verified, including that [1] passes and [1, 2] fails, and rest elements are how non-empty array types are written in practice. Options, hint and explanation need work.
evidence: tsc: rm-ts-31 `[1, "a", "b"]` and `[1]` → no errors; `[1, 2]` → TS2322 Type '[number, number]' is not assignable to type '[number, ...string[]]' (position 1: number not assignable to string)

options: number
string | number
any
rewrite.hint: pair is a tuple, so its size is fixed by its type. Ask how precisely TypeScript can state a length that can never change.
rewrite.explanation: A tuple type fixes its element count, so [string, number] has length typed as the literal 2, and const n keeps that literal. A plain array such as string[] has length: number, because its size is unknown to the checker; this literal length is one of the ways tuples differ from arrays. string | number is the type of pair's elements, not of its length, and nothing here is any. The same fact is available at the type level as [string, number]["length"], which you will meet with indexed access types.

rationale: The tuple-length fact belongs at this level but the type-level syntax does not; the value-level form keeps the objective and the key. The many flagged near-duplicates (rm-ts-122 and others) are outside this batch and were not compared.

objective: A fresh object literal assigned to a typed variable is checked for excess properties; unknown b is an error.
defects: hint is the generic fallback
stem 'What happens?' leaves compile time versus run time open

rewrite.hint: Structural typing normally tolerates extra properties. Ask whether an object literal written directly at the assignment gets that same tolerance.
rewrite.explanation: An object literal assigned directly to a typed target is fresh, and TypeScript checks it for excess properties: b does not exist in T, so the compiler reports TS2353 (Object literal may only specify known properties). This is what catches misspelled property names in configuration objects. The check applies only to fresh literals; assigning the same object through a variable, const wide = { a: 1, b: 2 }; const y: T = wide;, is accepted because structural typing then allows the extra property. Nothing is ignored silently and nothing fails at runtime.

rationale: Verified, including the via-variable contrast, and excess-property checking is one of the most practically useful rules at this level. Stem, hint and explanation need to be specific.
evidence: tsc: rm-ts-36 → TS2353 Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'b' does not exist in type 'T'; `const y: T = wide` (non-fresh) → no error

In plain JavaScript the same read would yield undefined, and that silent undefined is exactly the bug the checker reports early. If unknown keys are expected, declare an index signature such as { a: number; [key: string]: number } or use a Record type.

rewrite.hint: [key: string]: number is not a property named key. Ask what it says about every property name a value of T may have.
rewrite.explanation: An index signature { [key: string]: number } says that any property with a string name has a number value, so a and b are both allowed and no excess-property check applies to them. The word key is only a placeholder name, not a required property. The signature constrains values too: { a: "1" } would be TS2322. Use index signatures or Record<string, number> for dictionary-like objects whose keys are not known ahead of time.

rationale: Verified and practically important for dictionaries and lookup tables. Options need a consistent form, and the hint and explanation need to be specific.

rewrite.hint: readonly governs what may happen to a after the object exists. Ask whether the checker or the runtime enforces it.
rewrite.explanation: readonly a: number allows a to be set when the object is created and forbids assigning it afterwards, so o.a = 5 is TS2540 (Cannot assign to 'a' because it is a read-only property). The check is static: readonly compiles away, so no runtime error occurs and Object.freeze would be needed for real immutability. It also applies only through this type; the same object seen through a type without readonly could still be modified.

rationale: Verified; the concrete object-property case complements rm-ts-28 (tuple) and rm-ts-48 (interface, conceptual). Stem, hint and explanation need to be specific.

rewrite.hint: The argument is an object literal written straight into the call. Ask whether call arguments get the same freshness check as assignments to a typed variable.
rewrite.explanation: A fresh object literal passed as an argument is checked against the parameter type just like an assignment, so z triggers TS2353 (Object literal may only specify known properties). The same literal stored in a variable first, const arg = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }; f(arg);, is accepted because structural typing allows extra properties once the value is no longer fresh. z is therefore not silently ignored, and nothing fails at runtime.

rationale: Verified; it earns its place beside rm-ts-36 only if it teaches that call sites are checked the same way and variables are not, so the explanation must say so. Stem and hint need to be specific.
